Question for you: if Bolívar's Gran Colombia had survived, would South America look more like the US today, or would it have broken up anyway?

Sources for every number and date in the video, in order:

• The Spanish empire from California to the tip of South America (1800): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire
• The thirteen colonies' churches (Puritan Massachusetts, Quaker Pennsylvania, Catholic Maryland, Anglican Virginia) and their own paper money: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_American_currency
• 15 Spanish-speaking states by 1840, 18 today (Dominican Republic, Cuba and Panama came later): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_America
• Altitudes of Mexico City (~7,350 ft), Bogotá (~8,660 ft) and Quito (~9,350 ft): Wikipedia pages of each city
• The Andes, ~4,300 miles: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes · The Darién Gap and the Pan-American Highway: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darién_Gap
• Bourbon reforms: new viceroyalties of New Granada and the Río de la Plata (1776), captaincy general of Venezuela (1777): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourbon_Reforms
• Creole careers confined to their own administrative unit: Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities, ch. 4
• 1634: Philip IV bans all trade between New Spain and Peru: de la Serna Nasser, Histórica (PUCP), 2020 — https://revistas.pucp.edu.pe/index.php/historica/article/view/23273
• The new republics kept the colonial borders of 1810 (uti possidetis juris): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uti_possidetis_juris
• Stamp Act Congress, New York, October 1765, nine colonies: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_Act_Congress
• Abdications of Bayonne, May 1808: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdications_of_Bayonne
• The juntas: Quito 1809; Caracas, Buenos Aires, Bogotá and Santiago 1810; Hidalgo's Cry of Dolores, September 1810: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_American_wars_of_independence · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cry_of_Dolores
• Ferdinand VII returns in 1814; the war ends at Ayacucho, 1824: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ayacucho
• 1775: one Congress, one Continental Army: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Army
• The Portuguese court in Rio de Janeiro, 1808–1821; Brazil's independence under Pedro I, 1822: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_of_the_Portuguese_court_to_Brazil · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_of_Brazil
• The five attempts at unity: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Provinces_of_the_Río_de_la_Plata · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Colombia · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Central_America · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru–Bolivian_Confederation
• The Guayaquil conference, 1822: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaquil_conference
• The Congress of Panama, 1826 (four states attended; one US delegate died on the way, the other arrived too late; only Gran Colombia ratified): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_Panama · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_C._Anderson_Jr.
• Washington resigns his commission, 23 December 1783: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington%27s_resignation_as_commander-in-chief
• Bolívar, letter to Juan José Flores, 1830 ("those who serve a revolution plough the sea"): Bushnell (ed.), El Libertador: Writings of Simón Bolívar, Oxford University Press
• Intra-regional trade in Latin America and the Caribbean, 13.5% in 2024: Inter-American Development Bank, Trade Trends 2025
• Population of the 18 countries combined (~420 million) vs the US: World Bank, population 2024 — https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL
• The 11 Confederate states, 1861–1865: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America

comments.text: The 'one pin' thesis is elegant — remove the king in 1808 and eighteen countries fall off the map. I wonder how much weight you'd give to geography itself though: the Andes and the Amazon made a single Spanish-American state physically harder to hold together than the eastern seaboard. Great video.

comments.text:
Spanish speaking America was never truly culturally prepared to be a modern industrialized nation due to lack of European immigration. In the 1700s, The Americas and Caribbean colonies of Spain were actually wealthier than Britain's 13 colonies and Canada. Most of the Anglosphere historical establishment normally attribute that wealth to just gold and silver. But that is far from the truth because those Spanish colonies were much more economically developed than that. Gold and silver shipments from the New World to Spain had actually peaked in 1600, and by the early 1700s, those shipments dropped to about half. Despite that steep decline in precious metals output, Spain's Americans became wealthy. There was all sorts of industrial activities that included enterprises like metallurgy, ship building, textiles and many other industries. The Spanish colonies were so wealthy, that British merchants attempted to conduct risky illicit trade them and were very often abused by the brutal Spanish coast guard. By about 1730, the British merchant class became fed up enough with the choke hold of the Spanish coast guard and the losses they suffered from having their cargoes confiscated.  This frustration boiled over to the point they lobbied the British Crown for war with Spain.
The British Prime Minister Robert Walpole tired to tamp down the war fever, but by then war fever took hold and war was formally declared in 1739, known as the War of Jenkin's Ear.   That war a disaster for the British, but it speaks volumes about the wealth of the Spanish colonies. But when independence movements against Spain sprang up in the colonies circa 1810, the result was that the most productive people of the Spanish colonies fled to return back to Spain or Cuba. That was what we call today a classic  brain drain. Central and South America lost it's most productive human capital and the result was a devolvement into the impoverish societies we see today. Except for a few bright spots, most of Latin America never recovered from the Spanish withdrawal and never industrialized like the USA. Large Spanish multinational corporations even went on an investment spree in Latin America for a short while supplanting the USA in the early 2000s as the biggest foreign investors, but that too was mostly a bust. Latin American society for the most part just not culturally structured to be a modern industrial economy.
